nodes.title: Organisational Structure
key_items: Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited (AHEL); Apollo HealthCo Limited
nodes.summary: Apollo's organisational structure integrates specialised divisions under AHEL to deliver 'A Higher Promise.' The Hospitals Division provides tertiary and quaternary care with specialisations in cardiology, oncology, neurology, gastroenterology, transplants, and robotic surgery, including the Apollo Proton Cancer Centre and ZAP-X technology, contributing 52% revenue. Apollo HealthCo Limited combines pharmacy distribution and digital health services like Apollo 24/7 and Apollo Pharmacy, contributing 41% revenue. Apollo Health & Lifestyle Limited (AHLL) offers retail healthcare through short-stay facilities, birthing centers, multi-speciality clinics, diagnostic centres, dental and dialysis facilities, fertility services, and preventive care, contributing 7% revenue. AHLL's portfolio includes Apollo Diagnostics, Apollo Sugar Clinics, Apollo Clinics, Apollo Cradle and Children's Hospital, Apollo Fertility, Apollo Dental, Apollo Dialysis Centres, and Apollo Spectra Hospitals.

nodes.title: Clinical Excellence
nodes.summary: Apollo Hospitals emphasizes clinical excellence as a promise, with the ACE model founded nearly three decades ago on global standards. ACE 3.0 introduces appropriateness of care, ensuring evidence-based, judicious treatment choices. Apollo sets internal benchmarks 40-50% higher than global norms, particularly in emergency care and time-to-treatment. Innovation includes pioneering technologies like Proton Therapy and ZAP X Radiosurgery. The promise extends to all patients, ensuring world-class care across facilities, supported by governance and data-driven insights, positioning Apollo as a global leader in healthcare.

nodes.title: Success Stories
nodes.summary: This text highlights medical achievements: India's first scarless percutaneous Fontan procedure on a child, a rare cerebral revascularisation in a teen with AVMs, awake ECMO and bronchoscopy for a life-threatening airway obstruction, crossing 22,000 robotic surgeries, complete response of anorectal melanoma to immunotherapy, open surgical repair of complex aortic coarctation, 3D-technology-assisted mandible reconstruction with fibula graft, and successful mechanical thrombectomy for high-risk pulmonary embolism. Each case describes patient details, procedures, and outcomes, including milestones and multidisciplinary collaborations.

nodes.title: Technology
nodes.summary: Apollo Hospitals' digital transformation includes a Doctors' App for real-time information, AI co-pilot models for clinical workflows, NABH Digital Accreditation (Platinum at three hospitals), HR system transformation with a digital learning platform, and a real-time data platform for decision-making. Clinical AI solutions include risk scoring, decision support, predictive tools, and 12 algorithms for chronic conditions, with global certifications (ISO 13485, MDSAP, GS1). Cloud migration to Microsoft Azure and AI-enabled EMRs with generative AI summaries are completed. The Comprehensive Connected Care programme uses wearables for remote monitoring, reducing code blue calls and ICU readmissions. Strategic collaborations include AI-powered liver disease detection and co-pilot solutions. Ask Apollo is an AI health assistant. 5G ambulances extend care. Cybersecurity 2.0 includes MDR, SentinelOne, Fortinet, and a Security Operations Centre. AHLL's central reference lab offers automated, high-volume testing with faster turnaround.

nodes.summary: The section on India’s healthcare landscape summarizes Apollo Hospitals' Health of the Nation 2025 report, covering methodology using de-identified EMRs. Key health trends include cardiovascular risks with hidden calcium deposits; automation with AI and robotics; women's post-menopausal comorbidities; flexibility, strength, and balance as health predictors; mental health and sleep disorders like depression and obstructive sleep apnea; nutritional deficiencies in anaemia, vitamin D, B12, and protein; the triple threat of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity with age-specific prevalence; and early-onset cancers necessitating screening. It also highlights early-onset NCDs in children and adolescents from school screenings, and a vision of prevention, precision, and personalization as the new standard of care, including a Centre for Digital Health, Preventive and Precision Medicine.

It covers key trends: cardiovascular risks with hidden calcium deposits in asymptomatic individuals; the need for automation at scale with AI and robotics for efficient processing; women's health showing post-menopausal surges in comorbidities like diabetes, fatty liver, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity; flexibility, strength, and balance as predictors of future health; mental health and sleep disorders including depression and obstructive sleep apnea; nutritional deficiencies in anaemia, vitamin D, B12, and protein; the triple threat of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity with prevalence rates by age; and cancer's early onset in India necessitating screening. It also mentions methodology using de-identified EMRs from Apollo Group.

nodes.title: Early Onset of NCDs in Children and Adolescents
nodes.summary: Apollo SHINE Foundation screened 2.85 lakh students across primary, middle, high schools, and colleges in 6 states and 10 cities in India to detect non-communicable diseases (NCDs) early. Findings include 28% of college students and 8% of primary students overweight; 9% of high school and 19% of college students pre-hypertensive; and 2% of college students with elevated blood glucose. The text notes NCDs often begin in childhood/adolescence and can progress to severe complications without intervention. It highlights a vision of prevention through personalized care, and mentions the Centre for Digital Health, Preventive and Precision Medicine at Chittoor, launched with the University of Leicester, which uses digital health, genomics, and predictive analytics to intercept diseases before manifestation.

nodes.summary: Apollo Hospitals' Research and Development covers the Apollo Research Academy (launched September 2024) unifying AHERF, Apollo University, and Apollo Research Initiative under a five-year strategic plan focused on building research capacity and sponsored/investigator-driven research. Apollo Research and Innovation (ARI), India's leading Site Solutions Organisation, has conducted over 1,400 clinical trials across 23 operational sites with NABH and AAHRPP accreditations, and supports clinician-led research, device/technology validation, innovation incubation via the Apollo Innovation Centre, Apollo Innovation Quest, and Solvathon, plus clinical AI with 12 algorithms (2 patented). AHERF, a DSIR-recognised SIRO, houses a Class 10,000 wet lab (CMBRC) for liquid biopsy and pharmacogenetics, the Institute for EV Studies, and incubated companies with BIRAC grants. Genomics and precision medicine efforts include genetic screening, pharmacogenomics, molecular profiling, NIPT, and breakthroughs by the Apollo Genomics Institute. Apollo clinicians publish nearly 1,000 papers annually. The text also includes corporate overview references and annual report page numbers.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Provisions, Contingencies, Earnings Per Share, and Financial Instruments
key_items: Amortised Cost and Effective interest method
nodes.summary: The page outlines key accounting policies: provisions are recognized for present obligations and measured at best estimate, with receivables for expected reimbursements; contingent liabilities are possible obligations not recognized unless probable and measurable. Earnings per share is computed by dividing profit after tax by weighted average equity shares. Financial instruments are initially measured at fair value, with transaction costs adjusted unless at fair value through profit or loss. Financial assets include trade receivables at transaction price less impairment, equity investments at fair value (with irrevocable OCI election for strategic investments), and debt securities at FVOCI or FVPL. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with original maturities of three months or less. The amortised cost method uses the effective interest rate to allocate interest income. FVTOCI instruments are equity investments with fair value changes in OCI, not recycled to profit or loss, and dividends recognized in profit or loss.

It covers general information about the company and its business, material accounting policies including historical cost and fair value measurement with Level 1, 2, and 3 inputs, application of new and revised Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), a statement of compliance with Ind AS and the Companies Act, and the basis of consolidation. It also notes that financial statements were authorized for issue on May 30, 2025, and all amounts are in millions.

nodes.title: 3.2 Basis of preparation and presentation
nodes.summary: The text outlines the basis of preparation for consolidated financial statements, including historical cost except for certain fair value financial instruments, and principles of consolidation. It details control criteria: power over investee, exposure to variable returns, and ability to affect returns, with reassessment and considerations for less than majority voting rights. It describes consolidation procedures from acquisition to disposal, attribution of income to owners and non-controlling interests, policy alignments, and elimination of intragroup transactions. It lists subsidiaries consolidated as at March 31, 2025, with country of incorporation and percentage holdings for 2025 and 2024, including step-down subsidiaries, and notes contractual arrangements for control in specific entities and changes in subsidiary status during the year.

nodes.title: 3.4 Changes in the Group's ownership interests in existing subsidiaries
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting for changes in a group's ownership interests in subsidiaries. It covers two scenarios: changes without loss of control, treated as equity transactions with adjustments to carrying amounts and differences recognized in equity; and loss of control, where a gain or loss is recognized in profit and loss, calculated from consideration and retained interest fair values versus previous carrying amounts. It also addresses reclassification of previously recognized other comprehensive income and initial measurement of retained investments under Ind AS 109 or as associates/joint ventures.

nodes.title: 3.5 Business combinations
nodes.summary: The text details the acquisition method for business combinations, including measurement of consideration transferred at fair value and recognition of acquisition-related costs in profit or loss. It specifies exceptions for deferred tax assets/liabilities and employee benefit arrangements (Ind AS 12 and 19), share-based payment liabilities/equity instruments (Ind AS 102), and held-for-sale assets (Ind AS 105). It covers reclassification of acquiree's assets/liabilities, goodwill measurement as excess consideration plus non-controlling interests and previously held equity interest over net identifiable assets/liabilities, and initial measurement of non-controlling interests (fair value or proportionate share). It also addresses step acquisitions, remeasuring previously held equity interest to fair value with gains/losses in profit or loss, and reclassification of prior other comprehensive income amounts to profit or loss where appropriate.

nodes.title: 3.6 Goodwill
nodes.summary:
3.6 Goodwill
Goodwill arising on an acquisition of a business is carried at cost as established at the date of acquisition of the business (see note 3.5 above) less accumulated impairment losses, if any. For the purposes of impairment testing, goodwill is allocated to each of the Group’s cash-generating units (or groups of cash-generating units) that is expected to benefit from the synergies of the combination. On disposal of the relevant cash-generating unit, the attributable amount of goodwill is included in the determination of the profit and loss on disposal.

key_items: 3.8.2 Pharmaceutical, Fast Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) and Private Label Products

Pharmaceutical, FMCG, and private label product revenue is recognized at a point in time when control transfers to the customer, measured net of returns, allowances, trade discounts, and volume rebates. Project consultancy income from O&M contracts is recognized over time as services are received and accepted. Brand license fee revenue is recognized at a point in time when the licensee completes the contractual performance obligation.

nodes.title: 3.8.4 Services through digital platform
nodes.summary: The text details revenue recognition policies for Apollo 247's digital platform, covering subscription revenue, platform services, and diagnostics and consultations with variable consideration. nodes.title: Revenue Recognition Policies: Services, Contracts, Pricing and TPA
nodes.summary: This page outlines revenue recognition policies: Other Services covers project consultancy, clinical trials, franchise fees, other services, and royalties; Contract assets and liabilities define unbilled revenue and advance collections; Transaction Price addresses variable consideration, principal versus agent assessments for consultants and third-party providers; Contract modifications explain accounting for scope or price changes; Revenue from Third Party Administrator (TPA) details accrual-based inpatient services, contractual adjustments, and variable consideration.

nodes.title: 3.8.11 Trade accounts and other receivables and allowance for doubtful accounts
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for trade receivables, including recognition based on government reimbursement rates and contractual adjustments, quarterly review of doubtful accounts, and impairment assessment using historical default rates. It discusses collectability expectations and risks of increased allowances. It also covers dividend income recognition upon right establishment, interest income accrual using the effective interest method, and rental income recognition referencing lease accounting. Lease classification as finance or operating is explained, with details on lessor accounting for finance lease receivables and income allocation, and operating lease rental income recognition on a straight-line basis, including initial direct costs.

nodes.title: 3.9.2 The Group as lessee
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies: leases (lessee recognition, lease liabilities, right-of-use assets, short-term/low-value exemptions, variable rents); foreign currency exchange differences; borrowings and borrowing costs; government grants; employee benefits (defined contribution and benefit plans, leave encashment, short-term/long-term benefits); share-based payments (equity-settled and cash-settled); and taxation (current tax, deferred tax recognition, measurement, and offsetting).

nodes.title: Employee Benefits and Share-Based Payment Accounting Policies

3.13.2 Short-term and other long-term employee benefits

Government grants are recognized systematically, with asset-related grants as deferred revenue and expense-compensation grants in profit or loss. Employee benefits include retirement benefit costs (defined contribution and defined benefit plans, measured via projected unit credit method, with remeasurements in other comprehensive income) and termination benefits. nodes.title: 3.14.1 Share-based payment transactions

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Tax, Property, Plant, Equipment, and Intangible Assets

nodes.title: 3.17.3 Internally generated intangibles

nodes.title: 3.22.1 Financial assets

nodes.title: Financial Assets: Income Recognition, Impairment, Credit Risk, and Derecognition
